Two Clocks in One Portfolio: Twenty-Six Years of $SMH and $XLV

What public closing prices from 2000 through 2026 reveal when cyclical semiconductor innovation meets steady healthcare demand.

AV
Arthur Vance
Senior Portfolio Research Note · 2026-11-24 · 6 min read

If you study market history only through five-year bull windows, diversification always looks like a drag on returns. You have to widen the lens across full credit and inventory cycles—from the spring of 2000 through 2008 and 2022—before the real math of drawdown recovery reveals itself.

A portfolio that loses fifty percent requires a one-hundred-percent gain merely to return to its starting dollar balance. A portfolio that loses eighty percent, as pure Nasdaq and semiconductor holders experienced after March 2000, requires a four-hundred-percent climb just to break even. Avoiding the deepest part of the hole matters far more to long-term compounding than squeezing the final few percentage points out of an overheated rally.

Across public daily data from 2000 through 2026, $SMH (semiconductors) and $XLV (US healthcare) moved to remarkably distinct rhythms. Semiconductors captured the secular expansion of personal computing, mobile connectivity, cloud servers, and artificial intelligence, yet periodically endured thirty-five to eighty percent contractions. Healthcare compounded at a quieter pace, supported by demographics and recurring medical demand.
